summary.text: The Kuroshio, also called the Black Current or Japan Current, is a warm current that flows north on the west side of the North Pacific.
Like the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic, it carries warm equatorial water toward the pole and forms the western edge of the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre.
Its nutrient transport supports a rich fishing region, and its warm water helps produce and sustain typhoons.

facts.label: Name meaning
facts.value: Black Stream, for its deep blue water

items.prompt: The Kuroshio's name means 'Black Stream'. Where did that name come from?

options.label: Dark volcanic sand that it carries
The deep blue look of its water
Black seaweed floating on its surface
Storm clouds that darken it

items.explain: It was named for how deep blue its water looks.

items.prompt: Japan has the northernmost coral reefs in the world. What keeps them alive so far north?

options.label: Cold water full of deep-sea nutrients
Heat leaking from undersea volcanoes
Warm water carried up from the tropics
Bays sheltered from every winter wind

items.explain: The warm waters of the Kuroshio sustain Japan's coral reefs.

items.prompt: A typhoon forms where the current is warmest, near the equator. Where does it tend to travel next?

options.label: Toward the equator to gather more strength
East across the open Pacific toward California

Poleward along warm water until it fades

items.explain: Typhoons tend to follow the current's warm water poleward and die out once they reach colder water.

items.prompt: A sailor knows the Gulf Stream well. Which description would also fit the Kuroshio?

A cold current flowing toward the equator

A deep flow that never reaches the surface

items.explain: Both are powerful western boundary currents that move warm tropical water toward the poles.

items.prompt: The South China Sea's upper waters are fairly low in nutrients, yet parts of it show higher biological productivity. What helps?

options.label: Ice melt drifting all the way down from the Arctic
Salt building up as the seawater evaporates
Surface water sinking to the seafloor
Water pushed in by a big Pacific current

items.explain: Water from the Kuroshio intrudes into the South China Sea, and its nutrients raise biological productivity there.

The first map of Japan's coastline

paragraphs.heading: The Black Stream
paragraphs.text: The Kuroshio is a warm ocean current that runs north along the western side of the North Pacific. Its Japanese name means "Black Stream", and it also goes by the Black Current or the Japan Current. The name comes from the deep blue look of its water. It is roughly 100 kilometres wide, its surface averages about 24 °C (75 °F) across a year, and it often sheds eddies of small to middling size.

paragraphs.heading: The Pacific twin of the Gulf Stream
paragraphs.text: The Kuroshio does in the Pacific what the Gulf Stream does in the Atlantic. It is a western boundary current: a powerful current on the west side of an ocean basin that carries warm water from the equator toward the pole. It makes up the western side of the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre. The other sides of that circuit are the eastward North Pacific Current to the north, the southward California Current to the east, and the westward North Equatorial Current to the south.

paragraphs.heading: Its route past Japan
paragraphs.text: The current is born off Luzon in the Philippines, where the North Equatorial Current divides into a smaller southward branch, the Mindanao Current, and the larger northward Kuroshio. East of Taiwan it slips into the East China Sea through a deep gap in the Ryukyu islands called the Yonaguni Depression. It then follows the Okinawa Trough, the deepest part of that sea, and returns to the Pacific through the Tokara Strait. Along southern Japan it winds back and forth, and one branch, the Tsushima Current, turns into the Sea of Japan. At the Bōsō Peninsula it leaves the coast and heads east as the Kuroshio Extension, and off eastern Japan it joins the Oyashio Current to form the North Pacific Current.

paragraphs.heading: How much water it moves
paragraphs.text: The amount of water the current carries changes along its path and with the seasons. Inside the Sea of Japan, measurements point to a fairly steady flow of about 25 Sv, or 25 million cubic metres every second. Once it is back in the open Pacific it grows much stronger, reaching 65 Sv southeast of Japan, though this figure swings a good deal from season to season. Its sheer size, together with the shape of the seafloor, scours the deep bottom and moves sediment in several places. On the Kenting Plateau off southern Taiwan, for example, strong currents near the bottom, speeding up as the plateau rises, are likely what wears the seafloor away.

paragraphs.heading: Reefs and rich fishing
paragraphs.text: The Kuroshio's warm water keeps Japan's coral reefs alive, and these are the northernmost coral reefs on Earth. The current also carries large amounts of nutrients, which build a biologically rich region with varied food webs and an important fishing industry. The South China Sea shows this well: its upper waters are fairly poor in nutrients, yet it becomes more productive where Kuroshio water pushes in.

paragraphs.heading: A road for typhoons
paragraphs.text: Like the Gulf Stream, the Kuroshio warms the sea surface and loads the air above the western Pacific with moisture, and so it helps create and feed tropical cyclones, also known as typhoons. The western North Pacific sees about 25 typhoons in an average year. Most arrive between July and October, usually forming where the current is warmest near the equator. They then tend to follow its warm water toward the pole until they die out over colder seas.
